title: The Case of the Missing Sparkle-Stone
markdown:
The Grand Art Museum hummed like a happy bumblebee. It was the opening of the Sparkle-Stone exhibition, fancy coats swishing, voices bright as varnish. In the quiet cloakroom Iris the rabbit — fur like moonlight on snow — hung a plush velvet wrap so the collar sat exactly true. Beside her, Milo the mole sorted forgotten scarves. He liked dark cozy places more than the bustling hall, and the cloakroom had the decency to be both.

A sharp gasp, then a frantic whisper, arrived from the exhibition. Mrs. Thread, cloakroom boss, spectacles sliding, rushed back. “The Sparkle-Stone. Vanished.”

News spread like dandelion fluff. Panic did the rest. Iris’s long ears drooped. Her tidy world felt as if someone had shaken the drawer. Milo’s paws went clammy. Worried faces made a flutter in his tummy that no amount of scarf-folding could flatten.

“We must find it,” Mrs. Thread said. “The show cannot go on without it. Artists will be heartbroken, and the visitors have already begun feeling unlucky on purpose.”

Iris and Milo looked at each other. It was up to them, which was not a sentence either of them enjoyed. They peeked from the cloakroom. The main hall was a swirl of confused brows. “We check here again,” Iris whispered, though she knew every hook by heart. Milo nodded, dark eyes on the floor. He caught a faint scent of damp wool.

They peered under benches and behind hats, then under a second bench Iris had already declared innocent, because panic makes you check the same hook twice. Visitors shrugged or mumbled about glittery things in general, which is not a useful category. A woman in a feathered hat swore she had seen a gleam near the watercolours; it turned out to be a brooch she had forgotten she was wearing. A grumpy man pointed them toward a room of serious paintings, as if seriousness were a clue. Milo followed the wool scent instead, nose low, and it led past a rack of damp coats to a tall stack of forgotten umbrellas by a side door. One big umbrella, slightly open, looked like a dark rumbling cave. The wool smell was stronger there, mixed with rubber and last week’s rain.

Iris froze. The pile wobbled. She imagined a clatter, a spill of fabric and metal, the sort of mess that would take a week to apologise for. Her paws would not move closer.

“Just a quick look,” Milo said, a soft rumble. He nudged. The umbrellas argued among themselves. Iris’s heart thumped. She squeezed her eyes shut, wished for neatness, then remembered Mrs. Thread’s face and the artists who had hung their hopes on a stone. She hopped forward. Her paws landed on a damp rubbery handle. Sticky.

She moved the umbrella. Something small and smooth rolled out: the Sparkle-Stone, glittering, landed inside a long grey glove. The glove looked grubby and squashed. Iris’s fur bristled. A glove. Inside a glove. The lining was cold, a little damp, old perfume and dust. Her paws hovered. The stone was heavy with other people’s evening. The glove was a mess she would not have allowed in the cloakroom on a dare.

“The show,” she told herself, ears twitching, and reached in.

The lining was a slick texture that made her fur prickle. She gripped the stone and pulled it free, leaving the glove where it had failed as a hiding place. The feel clung to her paw. A small price, and she knew it, and she still wanted a wash.

They raced to Mrs. Thread. “We found it.” Mrs. Thread’s face lit like a hundred lamps that had been waiting for a switch. The Sparkle-Stone went back to its pedestal. The exhibition remembered how to buzz.

Later, last visitors gone, Iris saw Milo looking at the quiet hall. A single umbrella lay tipped near the side door. The old flicker arrived. She hopped over and righted it — not perfectly straight, not a spill. Her paw no longer ached from the glove. A quiet accomplishment sat in her chest instead. Milo sighed, the happy kind.

She logged damp wool / umbrella cave / glove lining in the cloakroom book, left the grey glove in the lost-and-found with a note that said contained a stone, and let Milo fold one last scarf as if folding were a way of putting the evening back. Mrs. Thread brought them each a biscuit from the staff tin, the sort that exists for crises, and did not ask them to make a speech. The museum, a little untidy and still open tomorrow, held. Iris’s ears, at last, came up.
